newsitem.title: GERMANY: Folders and files document horrors of Nazi era.
newsitem.headline: Folders and files document horrors of Nazi era.

text.p: From the outside Germany's centre for investigations of Nazi crimes looks like a grand country house set back off the main road, but inside it has a more sinister air.
Each of the many closed doors lining a long corridor bear the innocuous title "file room." Inside, however, endless paper folders and card indexes document the horrors of the Nazi era.
The damning documents will stay there after German justice ministers decided on Thursday to keep the threatened centre open, despite a dwindling number of war crimes investigations.

The 25 workers were relieved to hear Germany has decided to maintain the centre where it is after all investigations have ended, turning it into a public research centre rather than handing its files over to another institution.

The registry in this small town in southwest Germany has been open since 1958 and for nearly forty years has gathered copies of documents held by Poland, Russia and other countries as well as eyewitness accounts and transcriptions of trials.

One file holds a report by "Standartenfuehrer" (colonel) Karl Jaeger in 1943 about executions carried out in Riga. It offers an example of the methodical way the Nazis kept track of their crimes, leaving behind chilling evidence.

"Total executions: 138,272 of which 136,421 Jews," Jaeger's report said. He went on to list the number of women (55,556), children (34,464), Communists, Poles, mentally ill and partisans who were killed in Lithuania before December 1, 1942.
"I can today confirm that the Jewish problem in Lithuania has been solved by EK3 (commando unit number)," reported Jaeger.

"In Lithuania there are no more Jews except for worker Jews and their families...These Jews and their families must not be shot," he added, referring to Jews who were forced to labour until they died.
Jaeger hanged himself on the night of June 21, 1959, according to one of 1.5 million index cards in the centre.
The centre has been instrumental in helping local prosecutors throughout Germany gather evidence used against Nazi war criminals.
To date the investigators and prosecutors at Ludwigsburg have carried out more than 7,000 investigations. About 35 of them are still ongoing, said director Willi Dressen.

The future of the centre, which is funded by the states, was in doubt because the number of Nazi trials has dwindled and its long-time director Albert Streim died this summer. Last year it cost 2.2 million marks ($1.46 million) to run.

"Our mood is really positive," Dressen told Reuters. "For us it is of course better if the centre continues to run the way it has operated up to now. We were always in favour of keeping the centre in Ludwigsburg."
Around 300 people visit the archives each year, mainly historians but also school groups who come to conduct research.
At their disposal are many thousands of files and a massive card index which they can search by name, location of a particular crime or by military unit.
Around 650,000 names are listed on the cards.
But one room remains closed to the public. It holds files containing letters from relatives of former Nazi criminals.
Many have written to ask what their fathers did during the Second World War.
"Sometimes we tell them, but often we don't because it would be too traumatic for them to hear the details of what their relatives actually did," said Judge Herbert Schneider.
